highlights: Saarinen landmark reborn with all-suite Mayfair glamour and a superb Asaya spa
description:
The Chancery Rosewood brings Rosewood's second London address to Grosvenor Square, in the heart of Mayfair and within easy reach of Mount Street, Bond Street, Hyde Park and the galleries, clubs and auction houses that shape the neighbourhood's polished West End character. Its setting is one of London's most recognisable diplomatic addresses: the former U.S. Embassy, a Grade II-listed landmark originally designed by Eero Saarinen in 1960 and reopened as an all-suite hotel after an extensive restoration led by Sir David Chipperfield.

The 144 suites, with interiors by Joseph Dirand, translate the building's mid-century authority into a calmer residential language of stone, warm metal, generous proportions and expansive windows. The original diagrid facade and rooftop eagle give the hotel an unmistakable historic presence, while a 700-piece art collection and art concierge place contemporary culture at the centre of the stay.

Dining is unusually ambitious for a London hotel, with eight restaurants and bars across the building. Serra brings Southern Mediterranean cooking to Mayfair, Jacqueline reimagines afternoon tea around more than 100 teas, GSQ works as a day-to-night cafe and terrace, and Tobi Masa introduces chef Masayoshi Masa Takayama's Japanese cooking to London. Eagle Bar crowns the building with rooftop terraces overlooking Grosvenor Square and Hyde Park.

Asaya Spa anchors the wellness offering with five treatment rooms, a 25-metre pool, sauna, steam room, hydrozone, movement studio and gym. Event spaces and private dining rooms extend the sense of a civic landmark restored for contemporary London rather than a conventional grand hotel.

highlights: Sky-high Cambodian glamour with Mekong views, ambitious dining and a dramatic Sora terrace
description:
Rosewood Phnom Penh rises from the top 14 floors of Vattanac Capital Tower, a 188-metre landmark in the capital's central business district, with broad views over the Mekong, Tonle Sap and the low-rise city below. The address in Daun Penh places it close to the Royal Palace, National Museum, Central Market and Independence Monument, while the tower's own luxury mall adds a polished urban context at street level.

The 175 rooms and suites occupy a sky-high perch with floor-to-ceiling views and a residential style that mixes contemporary lines with Cambodian art and crafted details. Accommodation ranges from 50-square-metre rooms to spacious houses, including Monivong House and Norodom House, giving the hotel an unusual breadth for a city property. The 35th-floor lobby, art gallery and Art in Residence programme bring local creative culture into the daily rhythm of the hotel.

Dining is central to the experience. Brasserie Louis pairs French comfort food with Cambodian favourites, Iza serves Japanese izakaya cooking from robata grill, sushi and noodle stations, and Zhan Liang focuses on Cantonese, Sichuanese and northern Chinese flavours. Cuts brings steak, seafood, private dining suites and an extensive wine cellar, while Sora sits on a cantilevered terrace with a whisky library and one of the city's most dramatic skyline settings.

Sense, A Rosewood Spa, on level 33, adds seven treatment rooms and a nail studio, complemented by an indoor pool and fitness facilities. Meeting salons and The Pavilion support the business side of the tower, but the property's strongest identity is cultural and vertical: Phnom Penh's heritage, food scene and contemporary art reframed from the city's highest luxury address.

local_area: Ban Nadueay Village, Nahm Dong Valley
highlights: Bill Bensley jungle romance beside waterfalls, with Three-Key serenity near Luang Prabang
description:
Rosewood Luang Prabang sits in Ban Nadueay Village, on the green outskirts of Luang Prabang, within the UNESCO-protected Nahm Dong Valley. The resort is close enough for dawn alms-giving, temple walks, craft workshops and the town's French-Lao streets, yet its immediate world is quieter: forest, mountain light, flowing water and natural waterfalls threaded through the grounds.

Designed by Bill Bensley, the resort has just 23 rooms, suites, villas and hilltop tents, each shaped around Lao heritage, French-colonial echoes and adventurous storytelling. Riverside rooms and suites sit near the water, villas open to decks and private pools, and tents climb into the hillside with a stronger sense of jungle seclusion. The result is intimate rather than grand, with handcraft, colour and theatrical detail balanced by the sound of the river.

The Great House is the main restaurant, built around farm-to-table Laotian and Western-inspired cooking, herbs and vegetables sourced from local markets and farmers. Elephant Bridge Bar occupies a creekside setting where elephants once crossed, serving cocktails with Lao herbs and spices, while private waterfall dinners create one of the property's most atmospheric dining rituals.

Wellness is led by Sense, A Rosewood Spa, where treatments draw on Lao healing traditions and the calm of the surrounding jungle. The pool, guided mountain biking, Mekong and Nam Khan river cruises, Pak Ou Cave excursions, temple experiences, textile encounters and visits to the ethical MandaLao Elephant Sanctuary give the resort a rare balance of retreat and discovery. Its Three Michelin Keys reflect a stay defined by design, cultural immersion and deep natural quiet.

highlights: Vertical Haitang Bay glamour with ocean-view rooms, rooftop pool and tropical coastal energy
description:
Rosewood Sanya stands on Haitang Bay on Hainan Island, a coastal resort enclave facing the South China Sea. The setting places it away from Sanya's busier centre, with a seafront walking trail, gardens, beach life and easy access to island excursions such as yacht sailing, golf and the large Nanshan Temple complex. From its elevated sky lobby and ocean-facing rooms, the resort is built around long views of water, palms and tropical light.

Opened in 2017 as Rosewood's first resort in China, the property takes a more vertical approach to island luxury. Its 244 rooms and suites all frame panoramic ocean views, with residential interiors, warm natural materials, stone accents and a restrained contemporary tone. Hong Kong studio AB Concept shaped the mood as quietly nautical rather than theatrical, while landscaped lawns, leafy walkways and outdoor spaces soften the scale of the building.

Five restaurants and lounges give the resort its daily rhythm. The Fishmonger is a market-style seafood restaurant with open kitchens and fresh catch, East Kitchen serves Southeast Asian comfort dishes, and Chop House offers Italian-style grilled dishes in a seaside setting. The Lounge is made for light bites and cocktails, while HAI-Infinity Pool & Bar sits high above the bay, pairing panoramic views with the drama of the resort's rooftop pool.

Sense, A Rosewood Spa, draws on indigenous plants and herbs inspired by the remedies of the Li people, supported by a fitness studio, rooftop infinity pool and broad event spaces. Beach time, sailing, golf, local Hainan food experiences and temple visits make the hotel both a polished resort and a strong base for exploring China's tropical island south.

highlights: Private-pool island villas where Ryukyu minimalism meets luminous Miyako Blue waters
description:
Rosewood Miyakojima sits on a secluded peninsula on Miyako Island, part of Okinawa's Ryukyu chain, overlooking Oura Bay and the clear turquoise water often described locally as Miyako Blue. The resort is removed from Japan's familiar city-and-temple circuit, placing its stay amid sugarcane fields, reef-fringed beaches, sea turtle habitats and the spiritual traditions of an island known as the Island of Prayers.

Opened in March 2025 as Rosewood's first property in Japan, the resort is made up of 55 villas and houses, each with ocean views and a private pool. Studio Piet Boon shaped the architecture around low-slung modern Japanese minimalism, Ryukyu limestone, natural textures and a quiet dialogue with the landscape. Villas range across cliffside, mountain, beach and rocky-shore zones, while the three larger houses bring two-bedroom layouts, high ceilings, terraces, barbecue areas and dedicated butler service.

Dining gathers around Nagi, Maas, Yukuu and Choma, with Choma Bar adding an intimate cocktail counter. Nagi blends Italian cuisine with Japanese technique and a longevity-minded approach; Maas looks to the surrounding sea for simple, fresh flavours; Yukuu serves casual dishes by the pool; and Choma gathers sushi, tempura, teppanyaki and yakitori in an open seaside pavilion.

Asaya Spa brings six treatment rooms, a yoga studio and fitness centre, with rituals drawing on Okinawan herbs, local sea salt and the region's culture of longevity. Days can shift from beach yoga, kayaking, SUP and snorkeling above coral reefs to pottery workshops, adan weaving, Ryukyu karate, sea turtle encounters and Rosewood Explorers activities for younger guests. The mood is polished but elemental: ocean, craft and Ryukyuan calm in equal measure.
